analysis.one_liner: Extends overtime pay protections to farmworkers for the first time.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote; it died in the Education and Labor Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal wage law has exempted farmworkers from overtime pay since 1938, so agricultural workers who labor 60 or 70 hours a week get straight time. This bill would have ended that exemption, requiring farm employers to pay time-and-a-half after 55 hours a week starting in 2022, then stepping down to 40 hours by 2025. Smaller farms with 25 or fewer employees would have had more time to comply, and the bill also repealed a set of smaller overtime exemptions in agriculture-related industries like sugar processing and cotton ginning.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 2 million farmworkers in the United States, most of whom are low-paid and many of whom work long seasonal hours without any overtime premium. Under the bill, they would begin earning time-and-a-half pay once their workweek passed the new thresholds, a direct raise for the workers with the longest hours.

how_it_helps.text: Requires farm employers to pay 1.5 times the regular rate for hours beyond 55 per week in 2022, stepping down to 45 hours in 2024 and 40 hours in 2025, ending a 1938-era overtime exemption [S2].
Gives farms with 25 or fewer employees a longer phase-in, with overtime requirements beginning in 2025 and reaching the 40-hour threshold by 2028 [S2].

Repeals overtime exemptions for agriculture-related employers including small farms, irrigation projects, sugar processing, and cotton ginning, while keeping the existing exemption for members of the employer's immediate family [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Farm operators and agricultural employers, who would pay time-and-a-half for hours beyond the new thresholds. Some of that cost would be passed to consumers through produce prices, and very small farms argued the change would be hardest on them.

drawbacks.text: The costs fall hardest on smaller farm operations with thin margins, which is why the bill gave employers with 25 or fewer employees a longer phase-in before the 40-hour threshold applied [S2].

Lowering the overtime threshold from 55 to 40 hours by 2025 would make long workweeks much more expensive; some farms could respond by cutting workers' hours, which would reduce total earnings for workers who rely on extended seasonal hours to make ends meet [S3].

The compliance burden for piece-rate and multi-employer arrangements common in agriculture is real, and workers who are in the country without authorization may find it difficult to enforce overtime claims in practice [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers themselves the benefit is direct and substantial: time-and-a-half after a long week is a meaningful raise in one of the lowest-paid occupations in the country, one that every other covered worker has had since the 1930s. The costs are real but manageable in design terms — the bill phased the thresholds in over four years and gave small farms five to seven years, which addresses the sharpest objection. The strongest honest objection is behavioral: employers may cut hours rather than pay the premium, and enforcement for a workforce that includes many unauthorized workers is genuinely hard. On balance this is a straightforward fairness fix whose main cost is money to farm operators.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the Fairness for Farm Workers Act on May 13, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1][S5].
64 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors, all from the same party; no Republican cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no report — and it never reached the House floor; the action history shows only the introduction and the referral [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm operators and agricultural employers kept the overtime exemption that has applied to farmworkers since 1938, saving them the cost of time-and-a-half pay for long workweeks. Farmworkers, who would have gained the overtime premium, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm employers kept the overtime exemption

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend overtime pay to farmworkers and recruited 64 cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor (Chair Robert C. Scott)
against.role: Committee of referral; controlled whether the bill got a markup or a vote
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — leaving it to die when the Congress ended

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: No House Republican cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no bipartisan base that might have pressed leadership to act

sides.party_line_note: All 65 supporters (the sponsor plus 64 cosponsors) were House Democrats and no Republican signed on, though the bill never got far enough for a recorded vote that would show where each party stood.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their exemption from overtime pay, requiring time-and-a-half after 40-55 hours a week depending on the year and farm size. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs directly against farmworkers' paychecks, which is the point of the bill.

industries.industry: Agriculture-related processors (sugar processing, cotton ginning, irrigation projects)
industries.note: The bill repealed their separate overtime exemptions under the Fair Labor Standards Act, so they would have owed overtime premiums they currently do not pay [S2].
